title: Packing More Into a Sentence
overview: Level 1 sentences were short because you had no way to join a description to a noun. This unit gives you that, and it is the largest single jump in what you can express: relative clauses let one sentence carry what previously took three. It also covers the comma rule, which is not decoration — in a relative clause a comma changes what the sentence means. It ends with a contract clause and its plain-English rewrite.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns and they build in order.
Open Patterns. Card 2 is the one where a comma changes the meaning.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a contract clause rewritten.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the diagnostic — the comma test.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
This unit is the biggest jump in Level 2, because it changes the length of the sentences you can produce.
In Level 1, if you wanted to say something about a noun, you had two options: an adjective in front of it, or a separate sentence after it. The man was tall. The man worked here. Two sentences, and the connection between them is left to the listener.
A relative clause joins them. The man who worked here was tall.
First pattern: defining relative clauses. These identify which one you mean.
The pronouns: who for people, which for things, that for either.
The man who worked here. The report which arrived yesterday. The report that arrived yesterday.
That is worth a word. In defining clauses, that is used constantly and is often preferred in speech, for both people and things. The man that worked here is perfectly normal English.
Here is what makes these clauses defining: remove the clause and you no longer know which one is meant.
The report which arrived yesterday is on my desk. Remove the clause: the report is on my desk. Which report? The sentence has lost the information that identified it.
That is the test, and it decides the comma rule on the next card.
One more thing about defining clauses, and it is the most useful piece of grammar in this unit. When the relative pronoun is the object of its clause, you can leave it out entirely.
The report that I read yesterday. The report I read yesterday.
Both correct, and the second is what people actually say.
But you cannot drop it when it is the subject. The report that arrived yesterday. The report arrived yesterday — that is now a different sentence entirely.
The test: is there a subject already inside the clause? In the report I read yesterday, I is the subject, so that was the object and can go. In the report that arrived yesterday, there is no other subject, so that is the subject and must stay.
Second pattern: non-defining clauses, and the comma.
A non-defining clause adds information you did not need in order to identify the noun.
My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, is retiring.
You already know which person is meant — my manager. The clause adds something extra, and it sits between commas.
Now the reason this matters, and it is the clearest case in English of punctuation carrying meaning.
My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. No commas. Defining. It tells you which brother — the one in Manchester — and it implies I have more than one.
My brother, who lives in Manchester, is coming. Commas. Non-defining. I have one brother, and by the way he lives in Manchester.
Same words, different punctuation, genuinely different facts about my family.
Two rules for non-defining clauses. You cannot use that — it must be who or which. And you cannot leave the pronoun out.
Third pattern: where and whose.
Where replaces a relative clause about a place. The building where I work. That is shorter than the building in which I work and it is what people say.
Whose shows possession, and it works for people and for things. The man whose car was blocked. The company whose contract we signed.
Whose surprises people because it looks like a question word from Level 1 Unit 16. It is doing a completely different job here, and it is the only relative pronoun that shows possession.
Fourth pattern: complex noun phrases.
This is what all of the above adds up to. A noun phrase in written English can carry a great deal before the main verb arrives.
The report that I read yesterday, which was written by somebody who has never visited the site, arrives at the wrong conclusion.
Everything before arrives is the subject. That is one noun with three clauses attached, and it is entirely normal in written English.
But here is the warning, and it matters more than the technique. A noun phrase that long is hard to read, and the reason is mechanical: the reader has to hold the subject in mind until the verb arrives. Every clause you insert makes them hold it longer.
So the skill is not building the longest possible noun phrase. It is knowing when to build one and when to use two sentences instead. Legal and official writing overuses this structure badly, and the plain-English movement exists largely to undo it.
The rule I would give you: one clause attached to a noun is usually good. Two is sometimes right. Three means you should probably have written two sentences.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: To say exactly what something means or includes.
words.example: The contract does not define what reasonable means.
practice: How do you define success here?
The term is defined in section 2.
Define it before you argue about it.
words.starter: The contract does not define what reasonable
words.tutor: Say a sentence defining something, using a relative clause: a X is a thing that…

words.meaning: To recognise or establish which one something is.
words.example: The clause that identifies the parties is missing.
practice: I could not identify the fault.
It identifies you as the account holder.
Two items have not been identified.
words.starter: The clause that identifies the parties is
words.tutor: A defining relative clause identifies. Say a noun plus a clause that identifies it.

words.meaning: To state something exactly and in detail.
words.example: The notice does not specify which entrance.
practice: The contract specifies who is responsible.
words.starter: The notice does not specify which
words.tutor: Say specify and define. One states detail, the other states meaning.

words.meaning: To show or suggest something.
words.example: The figures indicate a problem which nobody has explained.
practice: It indicates that the seal has failed.
The sign indicates the way out.
words.starter: The figures indicate a problem which nobody has
words.tutor: Indicate is weaker than show. Say the difference in one sentence.

words.meaning: To mention, or to direct somebody to something.
words.example: The clause refers to an appendix which is not attached.
practice: It refers to the earlier agreement.
words.starter: The clause refers to an appendix which is not
words.tutor: Notice refer takes to. Say refer to something three times.

words.meaning: To recognise the difference between two things.
words.example: The comma is what distinguishes the two meanings.
practice: It is hard to distinguish between them.
The rule distinguishes staff from visitors.
words.starter: The comma is what distinguishes the two
words.tutor: Notice distinguish between two things. Say distinguish between A and B.

words.meaning: A group of things that share a quality.
words.example: There is a category which the form does not cover.
practice: Which category does this belong to?
The category was added last year.
It does not fit any category.
words.starter: There is a category which the form does not
words.tutor: Say which category something belongs to. Notice belong takes to.

words.meaning: A kind or sort of thing.
words.example: It is the type of problem that only appears under load.
practice: That type of contract is unusual.
It is not the type of thing I do.
words.starter: It is the type of problem that only appears under
words.tutor: Say the type of thing that. The relative clause defines the type.

words.meaning: An important or noticeable part of something.
words.example: The feature that matters most is the one nobody mentions.
practice: That is not a feature, it is a fault.
The main feature is the size.
words.starter: The feature that matters most is the one nobody
words.tutor: Say the feature that. It is a defining clause, so no commas.

words.meaning: One part of a whole.
words.example: There is an element which has not been agreed.
practice: The human element is the difficult part.
words.starter: There is an element which has not been
words.tutor: Say an element which. Which and that are both fine in a defining clause.

words.meaning: One particular part or side of a situation.
words.example: The aspect that worries me is the cost.
practice: There is another aspect to consider.
It has a practical aspect and a legal one.
words.starter: The aspect that worries me is the
words.tutor: Say the aspect that worries me. Aspect is about a point of view; element is a part.

words.meaning: One of the parts a machine or system is made of.
words.example: The component which failed was replaced.
practice: The component is no longer made.
words.starter: The component which failed was
words.tutor: Say the component which failed. A defining clause, so no comma before which.

words.meaning: A person who applies for something.
words.example: An applicant is somebody who has applied but not yet been chosen.
practice: The applicant whose form was late was still considered.
The successful applicant starts in June.
words.starter: An applicant is somebody who has applied but not yet been
words.tutor: Define applicant using a relative clause: somebody who…

words.meaning: A person being considered for a job or position.
words.example: The candidate who arrived late was still interviewed.
practice: The candidate whose references were missing withdrew.
No candidate met all the criteria.
words.starter: The candidate who arrived late was still
words.tutor: Say applicant and candidate. One has applied; one is being considered.

words.meaning: A person or organisation that uses a professional service.
words.example: The client whose contract we signed has changed their mind.
practice: The client is always told first.
A client who complains is worth listening to.
words.starter: The client whose contract we signed has changed their
words.tutor: Say whose with a person and with an organisation. Both work.

words.meaning: A company that provides goods.
words.example: The supplier that we used before has closed.
practice: The supplier whose prices went up was replaced.
It is a supplier problem, not ours.
words.starter: The supplier that we used before has
words.tutor: In the first sentence, that is the object — try dropping it and say it again.

words.meaning: A person who lives in a particular place.
words.example: Residents whose parking is affected will be written to.
practice: The resident who complained was right.
A resident is somebody who lives here permanently.
words.starter: Residents whose parking is affected will be written
words.tutor: Say a resident is somebody who. Defining a role is what these clauses are for.

words.meaning: A person who takes part in something.
words.example: Participants who cannot attend should tell us by Friday.
practice: The participant whose name is missing has withdrawn.
words.starter: Participants who cannot attend should tell us by
words.tutor: Say participants who cannot attend. Defining, so no commas.

words.meaning: The building and land a business occupies. Always plural.
words.example: The premises where we used to work have been sold.
practice: The premises are locked at eight.
The premises where it happened are closed.
words.starter: The premises where we used to work have been
words.tutor: Premises is always plural. Say the premises are, never the premises is.

words.meaning: A building or service provided for a purpose.
words.example: The facility where the equipment is stored is unheated.
practice: There is no facility for that here.
The facility whose lease expires is the smaller one.
words.starter: The facility where the equipment is stored is
words.tutor: Say the facility where. Where replaces a longer phrase about place.

words.meaning: The place where an event happens.
words.example: The venue where it was held has changed.
practice: The venue whose booking fell through was the first choice.
words.starter: The venue where it was held has
words.tutor: Say the venue where. Compare it with the venue in which — one is normal speech.

words.meaning: A place where something is located or happens.
words.example: The site where the work is taking place is fenced off.
practice: The site whose access road is blocked cannot be used.
words.starter: The site where the work is taking place is fenced
words.tutor: Say the site where and the site whose in two sentences.

words.meaning: A single thing in a list or collection.
words.example: The item that is missing is the most expensive one.
practice: The item was damaged in transit.
words.starter: The item that is missing is the most expensive
words.tutor: Say the item that is missing. That is the subject here, so it cannot be dropped.

words.meaning: A piece of equipment made for a particular purpose.
words.example: A device that measures it costs very little.
practice: The device whose battery failed has been replaced.
words.starter: A device that measures it costs very
words.tutor: Define a device using a relative clause: a device that…

words.meaning: Exact and clearly stated.
words.example: The clause is not precise about who pays.
practice: It needs to be more precise.
words.starter: The clause is not precise about who
words.tutor: Say precise and vague in one sentence about the same document.

words.meaning: Not clearly or exactly expressed.
words.example: The wording is deliberately vague.
practice: That is too vague to act on.
She was vague about the timing.
A vague answer is not an answer.
It is vague rather than wrong.
words.starter: The wording is deliberately
words.tutor: Say deliberately vague. Vagueness is often a choice rather than a mistake.

words.meaning: Able to be understood in more than one way.
words.example: Without the comma the sentence is ambiguous.
practice: It is ambiguous, not vague — it has two clear meanings.
words.starter: Without the comma the sentence is
words.tutor: Say ambiguous and vague. Ambiguous has two meanings; vague has none clearly.

words.meaning: Stated openly and directly.
words.example: The contract is explicit about the notice period.
practice: She was explicit about what she wanted.
words.starter: The contract is explicit about the notice
words.tutor: Say explicit and implicit in one sentence about the same rule.

words.meaning: Suggested but not stated directly.
words.example: The obligation is implicit rather than written down.
practice: There is an implicit assumption here.
It was implicit in what she said.
words.starter: The obligation is implicit rather than written
words.tutor: Say what is implicit in a rule you know. Implicit things cause the arguments.

readings.title: The Word You Can Leave Out
readings.passage:
There is one thing in this unit that will make your English sound immediately more natural, and it is a deletion rather than an addition.
The report that I read yesterday was wrong.
The report I read yesterday was wrong.
Both are correct. The second is what people actually say, and a learner who never drops the pronoun sounds noticeably more formal than they intend.
But you cannot always drop it, and the rule is precise.
You can drop the pronoun when it is the object of its clause. You cannot when it is the subject.
The test is quick: look inside the clause and ask whether there is already a subject.
The report I read yesterday. Inside the clause, I is the subject and read is the verb. So the missing pronoun was the object, and dropping it was fine.
The report that arrived yesterday. Inside the clause, there is no other subject at all — that is doing the job. Drop it and you get the report arrived yesterday, which is a complete sentence saying something else.
A quicker version of the same test: if a noun or pronoun follows immediately, you can drop it. If a verb follows immediately, you cannot.
The report I read — I follows, so drop it.
The report that arrived — arrived follows, so keep it.
That test takes a second and it is reliable.
One more note. In defining clauses, that is used for people as well as things, and constantly. The man that works here is normal English. Some people were taught that who is required for people; it is preferred in writing and it is not a rule of the language.

readings.title: The Comma That Changes the Facts
readings.passage:
In most of English, punctuation clarifies. In relative clauses it does something stronger: it changes what the sentence says.
My brother who lives in Manchester is coming.
My brother, who lives in Manchester, is coming.
The first has no commas. The clause is defining — it tells you which brother, and it therefore implies I have more than one.
The second has commas. The clause is non-defining — it adds a fact you did not need. I have one brother, and incidentally he lives in Manchester.
Those two sentences make different claims about my family, and the only difference is two commas.
The test for which you need is the removal test. Take the clause out and see whether you still know which one is meant.
The report which arrived yesterday is on my desk. Remove it: the report is on my desk. Which report? You have lost the identification, so the clause was defining, so no commas.
My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, is retiring. Remove it: my manager is retiring. Still perfectly clear. So the clause was extra, so it takes commas.
Two further rules follow from this and they are worth memorising because they are absolute.
A non-defining clause cannot use that. My manager, that has worked here — wrong. It must be who or which.
And you cannot drop the pronoun in a non-defining clause. My manager, has worked here for twenty years, is retiring — not a sentence.
So everything you learned about flexibility in defining clauses reverses. Defining clauses are flexible: that or who, pronoun optional when it is the object. Non-defining clauses are rigid: who or which only, pronoun always present, commas always.
And this matters beyond writing correctly. In a contract or a notice, a missing comma changes who is covered by a clause, and that is not a stylistic question.

readings.title: One Clause, Twice
readings.setting: A clause from a tenancy agreement, and the plain-English version the housing officer wrote for tenants.
readings.passage:
ORIGINAL CLAUSE 7.3

  Any tenant who is in occupation of a
  property in respect of which a repair
  request that has been submitted in
  accordance with clause 7.1 remains
  outstanding for a period exceeding 20
  working days may, subject to having
  given the notice which is specified in
  clause 7.2, arrange for the works which
  are the subject of the said request to
  be carried out by a contractor whose
  details have been notified to the
  landlord, and recover the reasonable
  cost thereof.

-----------------------------------------

  PLAIN ENGLISH VERSION

  You can arrange your own repair and
  claim the cost back, if all of these
  are true:

   1. You reported the repair under
      clause 7.1.
   2. More than 20 working days have
      passed and it still is not done.
   3. You gave us the notice described
      in clause 7.2.
   4. You told us who the contractor
      would be, before they started.

  We will pay reasonable costs only.
  Keep the receipts.

  If you are not sure whether you have
  done step 3, ring us before you book
  anybody.

comprehension.q: When can you drop the relative pronoun?
comprehension.a: When it is the object of its clause. Not when it is the subject.
comprehension.why: The deletion is what makes the structure sound natural, and it is the single most useful thing in the unit.

comprehension.q: What is the quick version of the test?
comprehension.a: If a noun or pronoun follows immediately, you can drop it. If a verb follows immediately, you cannot.
comprehension.why: It is faster than analysing subjects and objects, and it is reliable enough to use mid-sentence.

comprehension.q: What does the text say about using that for people?
comprehension.a: It is normal English and very common. Who is preferred in writing, but the idea that who is required for people is not a rule of the language.
comprehension.why: Learners are often taught the stricter version and then hear the looser one constantly, which is confusing unless the situation is named.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between my brother who lives in Manchester and my brother, who lives in Manchester?
comprehension.a: The first identifies which brother and implies there is more than one. The second says there is one brother and adds where he lives.
comprehension.why: Two commas change a fact about the speaker's family. It is the clearest case in English of punctuation carrying meaning rather than clarifying it.

comprehension.a: Take the clause out and see whether you still know which one is meant. If you have lost the identification, the clause is defining and takes no commas.
comprehension.why: It works on any sentence and it converts a punctuation decision into a meaning decision, which is easier to judge.

comprehension.q: What two rules reverse in a non-defining clause?
comprehension.a: You cannot use that — it must be who or which — and you cannot drop the pronoun. Defining clauses are flexible; non-defining ones are rigid.
comprehension.why: Both are absolute, which makes them worth memorising rather than reasoning about each time.

comprehension.q: How many relative clauses does the original clause 7.3 contain?
comprehension.a: Six — who is in occupation, in respect of which, that has been submitted, which is specified, which are the subject, and whose details have been notified.
comprehension.why: Counting them is the point. The sentence is grammatical and the number of nested clauses is what makes it unusable.

comprehension.q: Why is the original hard to read, in mechanical terms?
comprehension.a: Because the subject — any tenant — is separated from its verb, may arrange, by about fifty words of nested clauses, so the reader has to hold the subject in mind throughout.
comprehension.why: The difficulty has a specific cause rather than being generally about long words, and naming the cause makes it fixable.

comprehension.q: What does the plain-English version do with the four conditions?
comprehension.a: It turns them into a numbered list, so each one can be checked separately instead of being held together in a single sentence.
comprehension.why: The rewrite does not simplify the rules — all four conditions survive. It changes how many things the reader must hold at once.

comprehension.q: The plain version ends with a sentence the original does not contain. What does it add, and why does it matter?
comprehension.a: It tells the tenant to ring if unsure whether they have completed step 3. It matters because step 3 is the condition most likely to be missed, and missing it means the cost cannot be recovered.
comprehension.why: The rewrite is not only shorter — it anticipates where the reader will fail, which the original does not attempt.

grammar.title: Defining relative clauses
grammar.explanation: A clause that identifies which one you mean. This is the structure that lets one sentence carry what previously took two or three.
grammar.rule:
THE PRONOUNS
  who    people
  which  things
  that   either - and very common

  The man who worked here.
  The report which arrived yesterday.
  The man that worked here.  <- normal

WHAT MAKES IT DEFINING
  remove the clause and you no longer
  know WHICH ONE is meant.

  The report which arrived yesterday is
  on my desk.
  -> "The report is on my desk." Which one?

  No commas, ever, on a defining clause.

DROPPING THE PRONOUN
  You CAN when it is the OBJECT:
     the report that I read  ->
     the report I read          natural

  You CANNOT when it is the SUBJECT:
     the report that arrived
     -> "the report arrived" = different

THE QUICK TEST
  noun/pronoun follows -> you can drop it
  verb follows         -> you cannot
grammar.workedExample:
You have two sentences: The report arrived yesterday. The report was wrong.
1. The second sentence is what you want to say; the first identifies which report.
2. Join them with a relative pronoun. The report is a thing, so which or that.
3. The report that arrived yesterday was wrong.
4. Can you drop that? Apply the quick test — what follows it? Arrived, a verb. So no; it is the subject and must stay.
Now a different pair: I read the report yesterday. The report was wrong.
1. Join: the report that I read yesterday was wrong.
2. Apply the test — what follows that? I, a pronoun. So you can drop it.
3. The report I read yesterday was wrong.
That second version is what a fluent speaker would say, and producing it is the main practical gain from this card.
grammar.mistake: Never dropping the pronoun, which is grammatically safe and makes every sentence sound more formal than intended. The opposite error is dropping it when it is the subject — the report arrived yesterday was wrong, which is not a sentence. The quick test prevents both, and it takes a second.
grammar.tip: Noun follows, drop it. Verb follows, keep it. No commas either way.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair with a relative clause, then say whether the pronoun can be dropped.
1. The man worked here. He was tall.
2. I read the report yesterday. It was wrong.
3. The component failed. It was replaced.
4. We used that supplier before. It has closed.
5. The candidate arrived late. She was still interviewed.
6. You mentioned an item. It is missing.
grammar.answers:
1. The man who worked here was tall. — cannot drop; worked follows, so who is the subject.
2. The report I read yesterday was wrong. — dropped; I follows.
3. The component which failed was replaced. — cannot drop; failed follows.
4. The supplier we used before has closed. — dropped; we follows.
5. The candidate who arrived late was still interviewed. — cannot drop; arrived follows.
6. The item you mentioned is missing. — dropped; you follows.
Three could be dropped and three could not, and the quick test predicted all six. In every case, look at the word immediately after the gap.

grammar.title: Non-defining clauses and the comma
grammar.explanation: A clause that adds information you did not need in order to identify the noun. The commas are not decoration — they change what the sentence claims.
grammar.rule:
NON-DEFINING = extra information
  My manager, who has worked here for
  twenty years, is retiring.
  ^ you already knew which person.

THE COMMA CHANGES THE FACTS

  My brother who lives in Manchester
  is coming.
     no commas -> DEFINING
     tells you WHICH brother
     implies I have more than one

  My brother, who lives in Manchester,
  is coming.
     commas -> NON-DEFINING
     I have ONE brother.

THE REMOVAL TEST
  take the clause out.
  still know which one? -> commas
  lost the identification? -> no commas

TWO RULES THAT REVERSE
  non-defining CANNOT use that
     my manager, that has worked... WRONG
  non-defining CANNOT drop the pronoun

  defining   = flexible
  non-defining = rigid
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say your manager is retiring, and to mention how long they have been there.
1. Does the clause identify which manager? No — my manager already does that.
2. So the clause is extra, and extra clauses take commas.
3. Apply the removal test to check: my manager is retiring. Still clear. Confirmed.
4. Result: My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, is retiring.
5. Check the two rigid rules. Not that — who. And the pronoun cannot be dropped.
Now the contrast. You have two brothers and you mean the Manchester one.
1. Does the clause identify which one? Yes — without it, the listener does not know.
2. So it is defining, and defining clauses take no commas.
3. My brother who lives in Manchester is coming.
Same clause, opposite punctuation, and the difference is a fact about your family.
grammar.mistake: Putting commas round a defining clause, which quietly tells the reader you have only one of the thing. In ordinary writing this is a small confusion; in a contract or a notice it changes who is covered. The other error is using that with commas, which is simply not available.
grammar.tip: Removal test. Still clear, use commas. Lost the identification, no commas.
grammar.practice:
Add commas where they are needed, and say what each version means.
1. My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. (you have one brother)
2. My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. (you have three brothers)
3. My manager who has worked here for twenty years is retiring. (you have one manager)
4. The report which arrived yesterday is on my desk. (several reports arrived this week)
5. Our office which was refurbished last year is too small. (one office)
6. The candidate who arrived late was still interviewed. (several candidates)
grammar.answers:
1. My brother, who lives in Manchester, is coming. — one brother; the clause is extra.
2. My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. — three brothers; the clause says which.
3. My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, is retiring. — one manager, so extra.
4. The report which arrived yesterday is on my desk. — several reports, so the clause identifies; no commas.
5. Our office, which was refurbished last year, is too small. — one office, so extra.
6. The candidate who arrived late was still interviewed. — several candidates, so identifying; no commas.
Numbers 1 and 2 are the same words with different punctuation and different facts behind them. If you can produce that pair on demand, this card is secure.
Check that none of your comma versions uses that — non-defining clauses cannot.

grammar.title: Where and whose
grammar.explanation: Two more relative words. Where handles places, and whose is the only one that shows possession — for people and for things alike.
grammar.rule:
WHERE - for places
  The building where I work.
  The facility where it is stored.

  It replaces a longer phrase:
     the building in which I work
     ^ correct, formal, and not what
       people say.

WHOSE - possession
  works for PEOPLE:
     The man whose car was blocked.
     The candidate whose references
     were missing.

  and for THINGS:
     The company whose contract we signed.
     The site whose access road is blocked.

  It is the ONLY relative pronoun that
  shows possession.

NOT THE QUESTION WORD
  Whose is this?   <- Level 1 Unit 16
  the man whose car <- a different job

WHOSE CAN NEVER BE DROPPED.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to identify a man by the fact that his car was blocked.
1. The relationship is possession — the car belongs to him.
2. Possession takes whose, and it is the only option.
3. The man whose car was blocked.
4. Note that whose is followed immediately by the thing possessed, with no the: whose car, not whose the car.
Now a place. You want to say the building you work in has been sold.
1. The relationship is location.
2. Where handles it: the building where I work.
3. Result: The building where I work has been sold.
Compare the formal alternative, the building in which I work. It is correct and it belongs in a contract. Where is what you say.
And one that surprises people: whose works for things too. The company whose contract we signed. There is no separate word for non-human possession, so whose covers both.
grammar.mistake: Avoiding whose for things because it looks like it should only apply to people, and producing the company which its contract we signed, which is not English. Whose covers both. The other error is where after a noun that is not a place: the meeting where we decided is acceptable, but the report where it says is not — that needs in which or where it says becomes the report that says.
grammar.tip: Where for places. Whose for possession, people and things alike.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair using where or whose.
1. The building has been sold. I work in it.
2. The man complained. His car was blocked.
3. The company has gone. We signed its contract.
4. The facility is unheated. The equipment is stored there.
5. The candidate withdrew. Her references were missing.
6. The site cannot be used. Its access road is blocked.
grammar.answers:
1. The building where I work has been sold.
2. The man whose car was blocked complained.
3. The company whose contract we signed has gone.
4. The facility where the equipment is stored is unheated.
5. The candidate whose references were missing withdrew.
6. The site whose access road is blocked cannot be used.
Numbers 3 and 6 use whose for things — a company and a site. That is correct and it is the use learners avoid unnecessarily.
In every whose sentence, the possessed thing follows immediately with no article: whose car, whose contract, whose references, whose access road.

grammar.title: Complex noun phrases
grammar.explanation: What the first three cards add up to, and a warning about it. A noun phrase can carry several clauses before the main verb arrives, and knowing when not to is the actual skill.
grammar.rule:
WHAT YOU CAN NOW BUILD

  The report that I read yesterday,
  which was written by somebody who has
  never visited the site, arrives at the
  wrong conclusion.

  Everything before \"arrives\" is the
  subject: one noun, three clauses.

WHY IT IS HARD TO READ
  the reader must hold the SUBJECT in
  mind until the VERB arrives.
  Every clause makes them hold it longer.

  This is mechanical, not stylistic.

THE WORKING RULE
  1 clause on a noun  -> usually good
  2 clauses           -> sometimes right
  3 clauses           -> write two sentences

WHAT OFFICIAL WRITING DOES
  it stacks four, five, six.
  The plain-English movement exists
  largely to undo this.

THE FIX
  split into sentences, or into a
  numbered list of conditions.
grammar.workedExample:
You have this: The report that I read yesterday, which was written by somebody who has never visited the site, arrives at the wrong conclusion.
1. Count the clauses on the subject. That I read yesterday. Which was written by somebody. Who has never visited the site. Three.
2. Three means split it.
3. Find the main point: the report arrives at the wrong conclusion.
4. Put the rest in a second sentence: I read a report yesterday which arrives at the wrong conclusion. It was written by somebody who has never visited the site.
Two sentences, two clauses total, and the reader never holds a subject for more than a few words.
Notice what did not change: no information was lost, and no clause was simplified. The only change is how many things the reader must hold at once, which is the whole of readability in this area.
grammar.mistake: Treating length as sophistication. A three-clause subject is not more advanced writing — it is the same content arranged so the reader has to work harder. The genuine skill this card teaches is the split, and it is judged by counting clauses before the main verb rather than by feel.
grammar.tip: Three clauses on one noun means you should have written two sentences.
grammar.practice:
For each, count the clauses on the subject and rewrite if there are three or more.
1. The supplier we used before, which has now closed, was cheaper.
2. The tenant who reported the repair that was never done, and whose notice we have on file, is entitled to claim.
3. The item that is missing is the most expensive one.
4. The candidate whose references were missing, who arrived late, and who had applied twice before, was still the strongest.
grammar.answers:
1. Two clauses. Acceptable as it stands.
2. Three. Rewrite: The tenant reported a repair that was never done, and we have their notice on file. They are entitled to claim.
3. One. Fine.
4. Three. Rewrite: One candidate arrived late and her references were missing. She had also applied twice before. She was still the strongest.
In both rewrites, nothing was cut. The clauses became sentences, and the reader now meets one subject at a time.
Number 4 is worth reading aloud in both versions. The original is grammatical and you will lose the thread before the verb.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Join them up
speaking.instructions:
Take twelve pairs of short sentences about things around you.
Join each pair with a defining relative clause.
For each one, say aloud whether the pronoun can be dropped, and if it can, say the sentence again without it.
Record all twelve.
Play back and check you used the quick test rather than guessing — noun follows, drop it; verb follows, keep it.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor twelve pairs of sentences and ask it to join each one, then check whether it dropped the pronoun where it could.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Say the commas
speaking.instructions:
Say each of these pairs aloud, twice.
My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. / My brother, who lives in Manchester, is coming.
My manager who has been here twenty years is retiring. / My manager, who has been here twenty years, is retiring.
Do the same with four more pairs of your own.
Record all twelve.
Say the commas with a pause and a slight drop in your voice. After each pair, say aloud how many brothers or managers each version implies.
speaking.tutor: Say six sentences with and without commas and ask the tutor how many of the thing it thinks you have.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Where and whose
speaking.instructions:
Say twelve sentences about real places and real possessions.
Six with where — the building where, the place where, the site where.
Six with whose — three about people, three about things such as a company, a site or a device.
Record all twelve.
The three about things are the point of the drill. Whose works for things and learners avoid it, so if those three felt wrong, say them again five times each.
speaking.tutor: Say six whose sentences, three about people and three about things, and ask the tutor whether all six are correct.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Define six things
speaking.instructions:
Define six things from your own work or life, each in one sentence, using a defining relative clause.
An applicant is somebody who has applied but has not yet been chosen.
Use who for three and which or that for three.
Record all six.
Then listen back and ask whether each definition would let somebody tell the thing apart from a similar thing. A definition that does not distinguish is not doing its job.
speaking.tutor: Define six things to the tutor and ask it to name something your definition would wrongly include.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Split the long one
speaking.instructions:
Read this aloud: The tenant who reported the repair that was never done, and whose notice we have on file, is entitled to claim.
Notice where you lose the thread.
Now say it as two sentences, keeping every fact.
Do the same with three more long sentences — from Reading 3, or from anything official you can find.
Record both versions of each.
Play back and ask, for each pair, how far the reader gets before the main verb arrives.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor a three-clause sentence and ask it to split it without losing anything.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read both versions of the clause
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the original clause 7.3 aloud, all of it, in one breath if you can.
Then read the plain-English version.
Then say aloud: how many relative clauses the original contains, and how many words separate the subject from its verb.
Then say what the plain version adds at the end that the original does not contain, and why that sentence matters.
Record the last two parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor the original clause and ask it to list the four conditions a tenant must meet.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Twelve definitions
writing.prompt:
Write twelve definitions of things from your own field, work or daily life.
Each must be one sentence containing a defining relative clause.
Use who for at least four, which or that for at least four, where for at least two, and whose for at least two.
Then check each one against a test: name something your definition would wrongly include, and narrow it if you can.
writing.model:
1. An applicant is somebody who has applied for a post but has not yet been shortlisted.
2. A candidate is an applicant who is still being considered.
3. A supplier is a company that provides goods rather than services.
4. A resident is somebody who lives at an address permanently rather than staying there.
5. The premises are the building and land where a business operates.
6. A facility is a building where a particular activity is carried out.
7. A component is a part which a machine cannot work without.
8. A hazard is anything that could cause harm.
9. A defining clause is a clause which tells you which one is meant.
10. A non-defining clause is a clause whose removal costs the sentence nothing.
11. A guarantee is a promise whose period is fixed in advance.
12. An ambiguous sentence is one that has two clear meanings rather than none.
Narrowing: number 8 as written would include almost everything, so a better version is anything in a workplace that could cause harm and has not been removed.
writing.criteria: Twelve one-sentence definitions; at least four with who, four with which or that, two with where, two with whose; each definition distinguishes the thing from something similar; at least one narrowed after testing
writing.support: Write the pairs first — applicant and candidate, element and component, vague and ambiguous. Defining a thing against its near neighbour produces a sharper clause than defining it alone.
writing.extension: Take your three weakest definitions and add a second clause to each. Then decide whether the second clause helped or just made them longer.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Rewrite the clause
writing.prompt:
Use the original clause 7.3 in Reading 3.
Write your own plain-English version — not the one given.
Every condition and every entitlement in the original must survive.
Use a numbered list for the conditions.
No sentence may contain more than one relative clause.
Then write four lines: how many relative clauses the original had, how many yours has, what you added that the original lacks, and what you were tempted to leave out.
writing.model:
If a repair you have reported is still not done after 20 working days, you can arrange it yourself and claim the cost back.

All four of these must be true:
1. You reported it under clause 7.1.
2. More than 20 working days have passed.
3. You gave the notice set out in clause 7.2.
4. You gave us the contractor's details before the work started.

We will repay reasonable costs. Keep every receipt.

If you are unsure about point 3, ask us before booking anybody — it is the condition people most often miss.

1. The original has six relative clauses.
2. Mine has two: a repair you have reported, and the notice set out in clause 7.2.
3. I added the final warning about point 3, and the instruction to keep receipts is more prominent.
4. I was tempted to drop the words notified to the landlord in condition 4, and I kept it because it is the condition that decides whether the money comes back.
writing.starter: If a repair you have reported
writing.length: A rewritten clause plus four lines
writing.criteria: Every condition and entitlement from the original present; conditions in a numbered list; no sentence with more than one relative clause; four commentary lines; the reasonable-cost limitation retained
writing.support: List the original's conditions before writing — reported under 7.1, 20 working days elapsed, notice under 7.2 given, contractor's details notified. Four. If your version has three, one was quietly lost, and that is exactly how plain-English rewrites go wrong.
writing.extension: Give your version to somebody and ask them to tell you the four conditions from memory. Whichever one they forget is the one to make more prominent.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two versions
writing.prompt:
Use the two versions in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Why is the original hard to read? Give the mechanical reason, not just that it is long.
2. How many conditions does a tenant have to meet, and where are they in the original?
3. What does the plain version do with those conditions, and why does that help?
4. The plain version ends with a sentence the original does not contain. What is it and why does it matter?
5. Is the plain version simpler than the original, or only clearer? Explain.
writing.model:
1. Because the subject — any tenant — is separated from its verb, may arrange, by about fifty words of nested clauses. The reader has to hold the subject in mind the whole way, and each additional clause makes that harder.
2. Four: they must have reported the repair under clause 7.1, more than 20 working days must have passed, they must have given the notice specified in clause 7.2, and they must have notified the contractor's details. In the original all four are buried inside relative and participle clauses within one sentence.
3. It turns them into a numbered list, so each can be checked separately rather than held together. The reader can work through them one at a time and see immediately which one they are unsure about.
4. It says to ring if you are unsure whether you have done step 3. It matters because step 3 is the condition most easily missed, and missing it means the cost cannot be recovered — so the rewrite anticipates the reader's failure rather than only describing the rule.
5. Only clearer. Every condition and every limitation in the original survives in the rewrite, including reasonable costs only. Nothing was simplified; the same rules are arranged so that fewer things must be held at once.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 1 gives the subject-verb separation as the mechanical cause; answer 2 lists all four conditions; answer 5 distinguishes clearer from simpler and gives evidence
writing.support: Before answering, find the main verb of the original clause. It is may arrange, and it appears well over halfway through. Everything before it is the subject and its attachments, and locating that answers question 1.
writing.extension: Find one thing the plain version could be accused of losing, and decide whether the accusation is fair.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the ten mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. The report arrived yesterday was wrong.
2. My manager, that has worked here for twenty years, is retiring.
3. My manager, has worked here for twenty years, is retiring.
4. The report, which I read yesterday, is on my desk. (several reports; you mean that one)
5. My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. (you have one brother)
6. The building which I work in it has been sold.
7. The company which its contract we signed has gone.
8. The man who his car was blocked complained.
9. The tenant who reported the repair that was never done and whose notice we have on file and who has lived here for ten years is entitled to claim.
10. The item is missing is the most expensive one.
writing.model:
1. The report that arrived yesterday was wrong. (Pattern 1 — the pronoun is the subject, so it cannot be dropped)
2. My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, is retiring. (Pattern 2 — non-defining clauses cannot use that)
3. My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, is retiring. (Pattern 2 — non-defining clauses cannot drop the pronoun)
4. The report which I read yesterday is on my desk. (Pattern 2 — the clause identifies which report, so no commas)
5. My brother, who lives in Manchester, is coming. (Pattern 2 — one brother, so the clause is extra)
6. The building where I work has been sold. (Pattern 3 — where replaces in which, and it cannot be doubled with it)
7. The company whose contract we signed has gone. (Pattern 3 — whose covers things as well as people)
8. The man whose car was blocked complained. (Pattern 3 — possession takes whose)
9. The tenant reported a repair that was never done, and we have their notice on file. They have lived here for ten years and are entitled to claim. (Pattern 4 — three clauses on one subject, so split it)
10. The item that is missing is the most expensive one. (Pattern 1 — the pronoun is the subject and must stay)
writing.criteria: All ten corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 4 and 5 corrected in opposite directions; number 9 split rather than repunctuated
writing.support: Numbers 4 and 5 are the comma rule failing both ways — commas where the clause identifies, and none where it does not. Apply the removal test to each before changing anything.
writing.extension: Numbers 1 and 10 are the same error. Write two more, then two where the pronoun could be dropped.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Join and drop
activities.instructions:
Join each pair with a defining relative clause, then write YES or NO for whether the pronoun can be dropped.
1. The man worked here. He was tall.
2. I read the report yesterday. It was wrong.
3. The component failed. It was replaced.
4. We used that supplier before. It has closed.
5. The candidate arrived late. She was still interviewed.
6. You mentioned an item. It is missing.
7. The device measures it. It costs very little.
8. She sent a form. It has not arrived.
9. The client signed the contract. They have changed their mind.
10. I spoke to a resident. She complained.
11. The clause identifies the parties. It is missing.
12. He recommended a supplier. It was cheaper.
activities.answers:
1. The man who worked here was tall. — NO
2. The report I read yesterday was wrong. — YES
3. The component which failed was replaced. — NO
4. The supplier we used before has closed. — YES
5. The candidate who arrived late was still interviewed. — NO
6. The item you mentioned is missing. — YES
7. The device that measures it costs very little. — NO
8. The form she sent has not arrived. — YES
9. The client who signed the contract has changed their mind. — NO
10. The resident I spoke to complained. — YES
11. The clause that identifies the parties is missing. — NO
12. The supplier he recommended was cheaper. — YES
Six YES and six NO, and the quick test predicted every one. Look at the word immediately after the gap: a noun or pronoun means you can drop it, a verb means you cannot.
Number 10 keeps the preposition at the end — the resident I spoke to. That is normal English and Unit 18 of this level returns to it.

activities.title: Practice 2 — The comma test
activities.instructions:
Add commas where they are needed, and write what each sentence implies.
1. My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. (you have one brother)
2. My brother who lives in Manchester is coming. (you have three brothers)
3. My manager who has worked here for twenty years is retiring. (you have one manager)
4. The report which arrived yesterday is on my desk. (several arrived this week)
5. Our office which was refurbished last year is too small. (you have one office)
6. The candidate who arrived late was still interviewed. (several candidates)
7. My contract which ends in June has not been renewed. (you have one contract)
8. The supplier which raised its prices was replaced. (several suppliers)
9. Meridian Freight which employs about ninety people is expanding. (one company, named)
10. The tenants who reported repairs will be written to. (only some tenants reported)
11. The premises where we used to work have been sold. (one former workplace)
12. The component which failed has been replaced. (several components)
activities.answers:
Commas needed in: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
No commas in: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
1. One brother, so the clause is extra.
2. Three brothers, so the clause says which one.
3. One manager — extra.
4. Several reports — identifies which.
5. One office — extra.
6. Several candidates — identifies which.
7. One contract — extra.
8. Several suppliers — identifies which.
9. A named company can only be one thing, so any clause about it is always extra. Named things almost always take commas.
10. Only some tenants — identifies which, so no commas. With commas it would mean all tenants reported repairs.
11. One former workplace — extra.
12. Several components — identifies which.
Numbers 9 and 10 are the two worth studying. A proper name is already unique, so a clause after it cannot be defining. And number 10 shows how much a comma changes in a notice: with commas, every tenant gets a letter.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Where or whose
activities.instructions:
Join each pair using where or whose.
1. The building has been sold. I work in it.
2. The man complained. His car was blocked.
3. The company has gone. We signed its contract.
4. The facility is unheated. The equipment is stored there.
5. The candidate withdrew. Her references were missing.
6. The site cannot be used. Its access road is blocked.
7. The venue has changed. It was held there.
8. The client is unhappy. Their order was late.
9. The premises are closed. It happened there.
10. The device was replaced. Its battery failed.
11. The resident was right. Her complaint was ignored.
12. The office is too small. We meet there.
activities.answers:
1. The building where I work has been sold.
2. The man whose car was blocked complained.
3. The company whose contract we signed has gone.
4. The facility where the equipment is stored is unheated.
5. The candidate whose references were missing withdrew.
6. The site whose access road is blocked cannot be used.
7. The venue where it was held has changed.
8. The client whose order was late is unhappy.
9. The premises where it happened are closed.
10. The device whose battery failed was replaced.
11. The resident whose complaint was ignored was right.
12. The office where we meet is too small.
Five of the whose sentences are about things rather than people — a company, a site, a client organisation, a device. Whose covers both, and there is no alternative word.
In every whose sentence the possessed thing follows immediately with no article. Number 9 takes are because premises is always plural.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Count and split
activities.instructions:
Count the relative clauses attached to the subject. If there are three or more, rewrite as two or more sentences, losing nothing.
1. The supplier we used before, which has now closed, was cheaper.
2. The tenant who reported the repair that was never done, and whose notice we have on file, is entitled to claim.
3. The item that is missing is the most expensive one.
4. The candidate whose references were missing, who arrived late, and who had applied twice before, was still the strongest.
5. The report that I read yesterday, which was written by somebody who has never visited the site, arrives at the wrong conclusion.
6. The premises where we used to work have been sold.
activities.answers:
1. Two. Acceptable.
2. Three. Rewrite: The tenant reported a repair that was never done, and we have their notice on file. They are entitled to claim.
3. One. Fine.
4. Three. Rewrite: One candidate arrived late and her references were missing. She had also applied twice before. She was still the strongest.
5. Three. Rewrite: I read a report yesterday which arrives at the wrong conclusion. It was written by somebody who has never visited the site.
6. One. Fine.
In every rewrite, nothing was cut and no clause was simplified. The only change is how many things the reader holds before reaching the main verb.
Read number 4 aloud in both versions. The original is correct English and most readers lose the thread before was still the strongest.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Find a long one
activities.instructions:
This week, find one real sentence with three or more clauses attached to its subject — in a contract, a notice, a policy, terms and conditions, or an official letter.
Copy it out exactly.
Count the words between the subject and its main verb.
Then rewrite it, losing nothing.
Write one line saying what you were tempted to leave out.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your sentence.
What most people find: the sentence is easy to find. Contracts, insurance documents and council notices are full of them, and the word count between subject and verb is often over thirty.
The second finding is the temptation. Almost everybody wants to drop a condition or a qualifier — usually one that limits liability or specifies a deadline. Those are precisely the parts the original exists to state, and dropping them is how well-meaning plain-English rewrites become inaccurate. If you were tempted to cut something, that is the part to make more prominent rather than less.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Listen for the dropped pronoun
activities.instructions:
This week, listen for defining relative clauses in real speech.
Write down six exactly as you heard them.
For each, note whether the speaker used a pronoun or dropped it, and whether they used that or who for a person.
Then note how many non-defining clauses you heard at all.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: the pronoun is dropped nearly every time it can be. Speakers say the report I read and the person I spoke to almost without exception, and hearing that is more convincing than being told it.
The second finding is about that for people. You will hear the man that works here regularly, from fluent speakers, and it is normal English. If you were taught that who is required, this is where you find out otherwise.
The third finding is the interesting one. Non-defining clauses are much rarer in speech than in writing, because the commas are hard to hear and speakers use a separate sentence instead. That is worth knowing: the comma rule matters most when you write.

options: The report that arrived yesterday was wrong.
The report arrived yesterday was wrong.
The report, that arrived yesterday, was wrong.
The report which arrived yesterday, was wrong.
quizzes.a: The report that arrived yesterday was wrong.
quizzes.why: The pronoun is the subject of its clause, so it cannot be dropped. And a defining clause takes no commas.

quizzes.q: In which sentence can the pronoun be dropped?
options: The man who worked here was tall.
The report that I read yesterday was wrong.
The candidate who arrived late was interviewed.
The component which failed was replaced.
quizzes.a: The report that I read yesterday was wrong.
quizzes.why: A pronoun follows — I — so that is the object and can go. In the other three a verb follows, which means the pronoun is the subject.

quizzes.q: What is the quick test for dropping the pronoun?
options: If the noun is a person, drop it
If the sentence is long, drop it
If a noun or pronoun follows immediately, you can drop it
If it is which rather than that, drop it
quizzes.a: If a noun or pronoun follows immediately, you can drop it
quizzes.why: A verb following means the pronoun is the subject and must stay. The test takes a second and it is reliable.

quizzes.q: My brother, who lives in Manchester, is coming. What does this imply?
options: Nothing about how many brothers you have
You have more than one brother
Your brother is visiting Manchester
You have one brother
quizzes.why: The commas make the clause non-defining, so it is extra information rather than identification. Without commas it would tell you which brother and imply there are others.

options: My manager, that has worked here for twenty years, is retiring.
The report which arrived yesterday is on my desk.
My manager, who has worked here for twenty years, is retiring.
The report I read yesterday is on my desk.
quizzes.a: My manager, that has worked here for twenty years, is retiring.
quizzes.why: A non-defining clause cannot use that. It must be who or which, and the pronoun can never be dropped either.

quizzes.q: What is the removal test for?
options: Deciding between who and which
Deciding whether to use commas
Shortening a sentence
Finding the main verb
quizzes.why: Take the clause out. If you still know which one is meant, the clause is extra and takes commas. If you have lost the identification, it is defining and takes none.

options: The company which its contract we signed has gone.
The company that its contract we signed has gone.
The company whose contract we signed has gone.
The company who's contract we signed has gone.
quizzes.a: The company whose contract we signed has gone.
quizzes.why: Whose shows possession and works for things as well as people. There is no separate word for non-human possession.

options: The building where I work in has been sold.
The building where I work in it has been sold.
The building which I work has been sold.
The building where I work has been sold.
quizzes.a: The building where I work has been sold.
quizzes.why: Where already carries the idea of in which, so adding in or it duplicates it.

quizzes.q: The building in which I work. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing is wrong — it is correct but formal
It is ungrammatical
Which cannot follow a preposition
It should use that
quizzes.a: Nothing is wrong — it is correct but formal
quizzes.why: It belongs in a contract. Where is what people say, and choosing between them is a register decision rather than a correctness one.

quizzes.q: How many relative clauses on one subject should make you split the sentence?
options: Two
Three
Four
Any number is fine
quizzes.why: One is usually good and two is sometimes right. At three the reader is holding the subject across too much material before the verb arrives.

quizzes.q: Why is a long noun phrase hard to read?
options: The words are longer
It uses formal vocabulary
The reader must hold the subject in mind until the verb arrives
It contains too many commas
quizzes.a: The reader must hold the subject in mind until the verb arrives
quizzes.why: The cause is mechanical rather than stylistic, and naming it makes the problem fixable — split the sentence and the reader meets one subject at a time.

quizzes.q: The plain-English version of clause 7.3 keeps all four conditions. What does that tell you?
options: It is simpler than the original
It removed a condition
It is less accurate than the original
It is clearer but not simpler
quizzes.a: It is clearer but not simpler
quizzes.why: Every condition and limitation survives, including reasonable costs only. What changed is how many things the reader must hold at once, not what the rules are.

teacherNotes.note: Four pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Practice 2 is the diagnostic and it supplies the context in brackets for every item, so the learner has to reason from meaning to punctuation rather than guessing.

teacherNotes.type: The dropped pronoun is the practical gain
teacherNotes.note: A learner who never drops it is grammatically correct and sounds consistently more formal than they intend. The quick test — noun follows, drop it; verb follows, keep it — is faster than analysing subject and object and works mid-sentence. Practice 6 asks learners to listen for it in real speech, where it is dropped nearly every time it can be, which is more convincing than the rule.

teacherNotes.type: The comma genuinely changes the facts
teacherNotes.note: This is the clearest case in English of punctuation carrying meaning rather than clarifying it, and Practice 2 numbers 9 and 10 show the stakes: a proper name can only take a non-defining clause, and in number 10 the commas decide whether every tenant gets a letter or only some. That is not a stylistic point, and in contracts and notices it is the whole question.

teacherNotes.type: Whose for things is the avoided form
teacherNotes.note: Learners assume whose is only for people and then produce the company which its contract, which is not English. There is no alternative — whose covers both. Speaking 3 and Practice 3 both load the non-human cases deliberately, and half of Practice 3's whose items are about companies, sites and devices.

teacherNotes.type: Card 4 warns against what cards 1 to 3 enable
teacherNotes.note: The unit teaches learners to build long noun phrases and then tells them not to. That is deliberate: length reads as sophistication to learners at this level, and the counting rule — three clauses means two sentences — is checkable where a stylistic instinct is not. The mechanical explanation, that the reader holds the subject until the verb arrives, is what makes the rule persuasive rather than arbitrary.

teacherNotes.type: Why a contract clause and its rewrite
teacherNotes.note: Clause 7.3 contains six relative clauses and separates its subject from its verb by about fifty words, so it demonstrates the problem at a scale no invented example would. The rewrite keeps every condition, which is the point of Writing 3 question 5 — it is clearer, not simpler. Practice 5's key names the real danger of plain-English rewriting: the parts people are tempted to cut are the deadlines and the liability limits, which is precisely why the original states them.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Practice 5 sends learners to find a real contract, policy or official letter, which may be their own tenancy agreement, insurance document or employment contract: no clause from a document about the learner's own circumstances should be collected, shared or entered into the app, and the task asks only for the sentence structure and the word count, not the subject matter. Writing 2 works from the clause supplied in Reading 3 rather than from anything of the learner's own, and that framing should stay.

selfAssessment.statement: I can join two sentences with who or which instead of saying them separately.
I can tell what my brother who lives in Manchester means, and how the commas change it.
I can say the building where I work and the man whose car was blocked.
I can read an official sentence and rewrite it so somebody could act on it.

assignment.title: Definitions written, and a clause made usable
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record twelve definitions from Writing 1, each one sentence with a defining relative clause, using who, which or that, where and whose — then for each, record one further phrase naming something your definition would wrongly include. Second, write the twelve definitions out, produce your own plain-English rewrite of clause 7.3 as directed in Writing 2 with all four conditions surviving and the four commentary lines, and add your full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3. Keep everything together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written work
